records.name: Andorra
records.summary_text:
Andorra is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. The 2022 Law of the Person and Family modernised the legal framework (unified civil marriage, and legal gender recognition provisions); the Ministry of Equality now obliges all companies to maintain sexual and gender-based harassment protocols. ILGA-Europe records only three bias-motivated incidents in the most recent annual review — a tiny absolute number reflecting a small, safe, tourism-dependent country.

records.name: Monaco
records.summary_text:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

records.name: San Marino
records.summary_text:
San Marino is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. There is no functioning legal-gender-recognition process (a resident-facing gap only), no criminalisation, no bathroom law, no border friction (open border with the neighbouring country of Italy), and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in this tiny, heavily tourism-dependent nation surrounded by Italy.

The score reflects very high de facto safety combined with minimal explicit legal infrastructure for trans people. For a visitor, no legal exposure is documented.

records.name: Liechtenstein
records.summary_text:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination based on sexual orientation is banned, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not included in any anti-discrimination legislation, and there is no legal gender recognition law; these gaps are resident-facing, and a visitor faces no legal exposure.
